name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Copper Glance Trailhead (3,800–3,810 ft, small pullout signboard, parking for roughly 7 cars) on FR 5130 (Eightmile Creek Road), follow Copper Glance Trail #519. The first ~1.5 miles follows an old jeep track/mining tramway grade (FSR 505) that served the historic Copper Glance claims — a gentle, steady climb through forest. Around 1.5 miles (~5,100 ft) the track passes the ruins of the Copper Glance Mine; the old adits and structures are hazardous and should not be entered. Just past the mine the route narrows to true single-track and fords Copper Glance Creek (~1.6 miles) near an old bridge that has partially collapsed — expect a careful boulder-hop or wet ford, and note the crossing is explicitly not passable for stock. Beyond the creek the trail crosses a stretch of burned-out forest with heavy blowdown that can slow summer travel considerably (early-season snow actually eases this stretch by burying the deadfall). Watch closely for an easy-to-miss, unsigned climbers' path splitting right off the main Copper Glance Trail below Copper Glance Lake/Basin — this is the cutoff onto Isabella Ridge and Big Craggy's southeast ridge, and it's frequently walked past, especially where snow patches obscure the junction. Take this cutoff up through meadows and talus onto Isabella Ridge, then leave maintained tread around 5,900 ft and climb open slopes toward the southeast ridge proper. Around 7,800 ft the angle steepens and the terrain shifts to tedious, loose ('garbage' rock) scree for the final push to the 8,478 ft summit; early-season snow cover on this upper scree is strongly preferred over the bare, ball-bearing talus of late summer. There is no reliable water past Copper Glance Creek, so fill up there (or at Copper Glance Basin/Lake if camping partway). Total car-to-car distance/gain runs roughly 11–12 miles round trip with about 5,600–5,800 ft of gain when West Craggy is tagged in the same push, as most parties do; Big Craggy alone is somewhat shorter but still needs at least 4,700 ft of gain.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling — retrace the southeast ridge/rib line used on ascent. Favor climber's right on the upper scree and rock band, where footing is comparatively firmer and there's less rockfall exposure onto anyone below; the loose 'garbage' talus here is the descent's main hazard, particularly when dry and off-trail. Several trip reports specifically note that early-season snow cover on this upper section turns the descent into a fast, controlled plunge-step (or glissade in the snow gullies below the ridge), and is generally regarded as easier and safer than picking down the bare, ball-bearing scree of late summer — but check runout on any glissade line before committing, since the gullies feed directly into talus below. Below roughly 7,800 ft, work back down to the small bench and continue the southeast rib downclimb; expect sustained, knee-jarring, loose Class 2–3 terrain most of the way back to where the route rejoins the Copper Glance climbers' path. From there, retrace the approach: back through the burned, blowdown-choked forest, re-ford Copper Glance Creek near the collapsed bridge, pass (but stay out of) the old Copper Glance Mine, and follow the old jeep track back down to the trailhead.
overview: Big Craggy Peak (8,478 ft) is the high point of "the Craggies," a pair of dark, blocky summits on the Pasayten Wilderness boundary in the Okanogan Range, 12.5 miles north-northeast of Mazama. It ranks 60th-highest in Washington and 62nd on the Bulger List, with 3,133 ft of prominence — the summit rises about 4,400 ft above Eightmile Creek in just 1.25 miles. Unlike most Pasayten peaks, access is comparatively easy: a maintained trail reaches treeline and a forest road reaches the base, which is why Big Craggy attracts less-experienced Bulger baggers despite its loose rock. It is almost always climbed together with its slightly lower neighbor, West Craggy Peak (8,372 ft), via a shared saddle reached from Copper Glance Basin.

name: Southwest Slopes
approach: From the Entiat River Trailhead (3,150 ft, end of Entiat River Road), follow the Entiat River Trail #1400, a well-graded but increasingly rough valley trail that parallels the Entiat River the entire way. At 2.2 miles (3,480 ft) the Anthem Creek Trail #1435 splits off; the crossing at 2.5 miles is on a solid wooden bridge. At 3.6 miles (3,745 ft) pass the Cow Creek Meadows/Myrtle Lake Trail #1404 junction, then the Larch Lakes Trail #1430 at 4.7 miles (3,780 ft), Snowy Creek Meadows around 6.1 miles, and the Emerald Park Trail #1230 junction at 6.2 miles (4,000 ft). Miles 6-12 cross repeated burn zones from the Tinpan (2006), Wolverine (2015) and Duncan Ridge (2014) fires — expect an exposed, dry, dusty tread with little shade. At 8.2 miles (4,330 ft) pass the Ice Creek Trail #1405 junction, and reach Entiat Meadows proper around 11 miles (4,600 ft), a good camp with reliable water. Continue past the Cool Creek Trail #1431 junction at 13.3 miles (5,060 ft) into upper Entiat Meadows; the trail grows faint and brush/deadfall-choked above about 14 miles as it nears timberline (roughly 14.5-14.8 miles, ~5,100 ft), the usual base camp for the peak. From camp, leave the trail and climb the open, south-facing slope/rib system directly below Buckskin's summit — this is a broad old avalanche path; the rib closest to camp carries the least brush and gives the most direct line, while an old, badly overgrown boot path toward the east ridge is generally not worth chasing due to extensive deadfall. Ascend scree and heather (loose, will be slick when wet) roughly 2,000-2,800 ft to gain the east ridge around 7,200-7,900 ft, then follow the ridge crest — narrow and blocky in spots with minor gendarmes — the final few hundred feet to the 8,127 ft summit. Water is reliable along the entire valley trail (Entiat River, Anthem Creek at 2.2 mi, Snowybrushy Creek around 5.2 mi, plus seasonal side streams) but there is no dependable water above the meadows once you leave the trail, aside from early-season snowmelt. Main approach-specific hazards: heat/sun exposure through the burn sections, navigation through deadfall on the upper trail and on any attempt at the old east-ridge boot path, and loose, ball-bearing scree and wet heather on the open slope below the ridge.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, follow the east ridge back down to roughly 7,200-7,900 ft, then drop off the ridge onto the same south-facing rib/gully used on the way up, picking your way down through loose scree and heather (roughly 3,000 ft of scree plus slick heather) back to the upper Entiat Meadows camp/trail. From there it's a straightforward but long reverse of the Entiat River Trail #1400 (roughly 14.5-15 miles) back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no technical rappelling involved — rope and anchor gear are not part of a normal summer ascent. The scree and heather are noticeably looser and more slippery on the way down than going up, and the burned, faint upper stretch of trail plus any deadfall-choked side paths are the main route-finding hazards on the way out; give yourself enough daylight given the ~15-mile, 5,000 ft round-trip scale of the day.
overview: Buckskin Mountain (~8,124-8,127 ft depending on survey source) is the high point on the ridge linking Mount Fernow and Seven Fingered Jack above Entiat Meadows, in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It is NOT a Holden/boat-access peak like its Railroad Creek neighbors — the standard approach is the long Entiat River Trail up the Entiat River valley on the east (Entiat) side of the range, making this primarily a multi-day backpack-and-scramble trip.

pins.name: Snow Brushy Creek to Aurora Creek

name: Southeast Slopes
approach: From the end of FR-5606 (the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, ~3,940 ft), pick up the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. This lower section sits outside wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal and commonly used to knock out easy miles. The first ~6 miles follow the North Fork Entiat River on a gentle, mostly forested grade, with the river itself as a reliable water source the whole way — top off here, since the route runs dry above. Some post-wildfire sections have significant blowdown; a few parties describe losing the tread briefly among downed timber and having to scramble back onto it. At about mile 6.1 a signed spur splits off to Fern Lake (Trail #1436) — stay on #1437. Around mile 7, at roughly 5,800 ft, the main trail bends sharply east and climbs switchbacks for about a half mile to a junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 at about 6,600 ft, roughly a mile southwest of Cardinal's summit and a useful timing landmark. The final approach mile above this junction is noted as steep and loose underfoot. From the open meadow/basin past the junction, leave the trail and hike east through sparse forest, then talus, toward Cardinal's west/southwest flank. For the Southeast Slopes line specifically, contour or drop onto the peak's western slopes and work south below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree to reach the gully leading to the notch between the north and middle (traditionally climbed) summits — the same scree-gully notch most parties use regardless of which flank they approach from. Loose rock is constant in the upper basin and gully, so a helmet is worthwhile and parties should avoid stacking up directly below one another. Round trip to the summit runs roughly 20-21 miles with about 4,700 ft of gain, so most parties do it as a long single day or a one-night backpack with camp in the meadows/basin below the peak. The trail crosses Grouse Creek on a log partway up, within one of the fire-damaged sections that has blowdown.
descent: This is a walk-down/downclimb — no rope work or anchors are needed on the Southeast Slopes line. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose scree gully from the notch back into the upper basin, then pick your way back down through talus and sparse forest to rejoin the North Fork Entiat Trail near the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction (~6,600 ft). From there it's a straightforward trail descent down the switchbacks to about 5,800 ft and out along the gentle lower six-plus miles back to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead. The scree gully is the main descent hazard — it's loose top to bottom, so descend deliberately, keep the group tight, and stay alert for rockfall triggered by climbers above. One trip report on this peak noted the descent taking roughly half the time of the ascent once back on established trail. No rappels are required on this route.
overview: Cardinal Peak (8,596 ft) is the highest summit in the Chelan Mountains, a remote subrange at the head of the Entiat River drainage, less than 5 miles from Lake Chelan. The peak has three summit points along its ridge; the standard route reaches the middle summit, traditionally treated as the highpoint, via a gully and ridge on the mountain's west side — though a June 2023 theodolite survey found the south summit is roughly 7 inches taller and is technically the true highpoint, reached from the middle summit by a short, exposed low-5th-class step that this route includes as an optional finish. The north summit is a separate, harder Class 4 objective and is rarely climbed. Roughly 95% of climbers use the same North Fork Entiat approach, camping in the basin below Cardinal, Emerald, and Saska Peaks before a Class 3 scramble with real exposure near the top.

The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass

name: Chockstone Route
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft) on SR-20, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, and locate the obvious chasm/gully between North and South Early Winters Spire on the west side of the formations. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base; expect to switch between rock shoes and boots/crampons if snow lingers in the gully.
descent: The standard descent uses four bolted rappel stations with a 60m rope, plus one rappel off a tree down the 5.0 slab near the start, located about 30m down and skier's-right of the summit exit. An older/original variant instead makes five rappels straight down the ascent gully, including one free-hanging rappel off the chockstone, through loose and windy terrain; this is considered slower and less pleasant than the bolted West Face option.
overview: Chockstone Route (II+ 5.7) climbs the gully and south face between North and South Early Winters Spire — the original 1950 first-ascent line up the peak. A low-angle slab/layback first pitch (often scrambled or simul-climbed) leads up the gully toward a massive chockstone, bypassed on the left via the 5.7 crux pitch, before chimney systems lead to the summit plateau.

name: West Ridge / Colonial Glacier
approach: Start at the signed Pyramid Lake Trailhead on SR 20 (small pullout on the north side of the highway, ~21 miles east of Marblemount and just past the Diablo turnoff, elev. ~1,150 ft; no parking pass needed, NPS backcountry permit if camping). Follow the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail — a well-used boot path through second-growth and old-growth forest — which climbs a steady, unrelenting ~1,500-1,600 ft over about 2.1-2.3 miles to Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft). This maintained-trail portion ends at the lake; everything above is climbers'-trail/off-trail travel. Pick up the boot path around the right (east/north) side of the lake and continue climbing, now through brush, heather, and talus, gaining roughly 2,000 more feet up onto the crest of Pyramid Ridge. A knoll around 5,400-5,500 ft on this ridge is the customary high camp/bivy — seasonal ponds and puddles here and near ~4,500 ft (reported dry by late summer in low-snow years) are the last reliable water before the glacier. From the ridge crest, follow the climbers' path along the ridge over several knolls toward the base of Pyramid Peak, then drop and traverse a mix of scree and boulder-hop terrain beneath Pyramid's crumbly north face to reach the flat 6,100 ft basin at the toe of the Colonial Glacier — this traverse is loose underfoot and exposed to rockfall from above, and is the route's main approach-specific hazard. From the glacier-toe basin, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the Colonial Glacier, trending southeast/east across the upper glacier (crevasses are usually well-bridged under seasonal snow but are present and have been reported as a hazard, along with cornices along the traverse toward the Colonial-Snowfield col that are invisible from camp below) to reach the Colonial-Snowfield col or the base of the historic Northeast Gully. From the col, leave the ice for a loose gully leading up onto the West Ridge, which is then followed via Class 3-4 rock scrambling to the summit horn. Total car-to-summit distance runs roughly 10-14 miles round trip (parties differ depending on camp placement) with the ~6,600 ft of gain split roughly evenly between the maintained trail, the ridge/scree traverse, and the glacier-to-summit push.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the east ridge back to the head of the Northeast Gully, then downclimb/plunge-step the snow gully back down to the Colonial-Snowfield col, drop back onto the Colonial Glacier, and retrace the rope-up glacier traverse and the loose scree/boulder traverse beneath Pyramid Peak back to the Pyramid Ridge camp, then follow the climbers' path and maintained Pyramid Lake Trail back to the car. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel-dependent descent — but on the class 3-4 rock near the summit ridge, trip reports document an existing rap station (a sling/webbing anchor around a rock horn, not bolted) that some parties use for a short single-rope rappel (roughly 20-30m, any single rope 30m+ works) over the steepest step; other parties simply downclimb this same section instead, since it's optional class 3-4 terrain for a confident scrambler. There is no other fixed or bolted rappel infrastructure reported on this route. Descent hazards mirror the approach in reverse: softening glacier snow and weaker crevasse bridges later in the day, loose rock in the gully and on the summit ridge scramble, potential rockfall on the Pyramid traverse, and the reported cornice hazard along the glacier traverse near the col — parties should time the glacier/col crossing for firm early-morning or evening snow rather than midday.
overview: Colonial Peak is one of the steepest-rising summits in the North Cascades, gaining roughly 6,500+ ft above Diablo Lake's Thunder Arm in under 2.5 horizontal miles. It lies in the North Unit of North Cascades National Park, accessed through the Ross Lake National Recreation Area corridor along SR 20, and shares its glaciated basin with Snowfield Peak, Neve Peak, and Paul Bunyan's Stump — a popular multi-summit basin for Mountaineers-style basic glacier climbs. The standard route (sometimes called the West Ridge) climbs the Colonial Glacier on the northeast side to the Colonial-Snowfield col, then follows the ridge over talus and firn to a short, exposed class 3-4 summit block. First climbed July 31, 1931 by William Degenhardt and Herbert Strandberg.
bivyNames: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col

name: Northwest Couloir / Eldorado Glacier
approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. The approach to this face is longer and more involved than the East Ridge approach — a long, somewhat complicated route across glaciated and crevassed terrain, so rope up for the glacier sections. High camp is typically established either in Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek Basin or higher at the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier site (~7,500–7,600 ft). One recorded ascent (climbing from the trailhead in a single push) took roughly 5 hours to reach the couloir's base; that party also used a shortcut of a belayed downclimb (~35 m) and two 30-meter rappels down a snow/rock gully near the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col to drop directly to within about 100 yards of the couloir, which meaningfully shortens the standard glacier traverse but is a variation, not the only way in — most parties simply continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft. Hazards on approach: crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glaciers, a long featureless glacier crossing that can be disorienting in whiteout, and the optional gully downclimb/rappel shortcut is itself exposed snow-and-rock terrain.
descent: From the summit, do not reverse the couloir — descend via the standard East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier route: downclimb the knife-edge summit ridge, drop through the gap in the lower East Ridge, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, then descend the Eldorado Glacier back toward Roush Basin and Eldorado Creek Basin, finishing on the timbered climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead (see the East Ridge route for full detail). This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappels required on the descent itself — one party even skied the knife-edge ridge and glacier on the way down. Rappelling comes up on this route only on the approach/entry into the couloir, not on the summit descent: one party used a 40-meter rappel off the Inspiration Glacier side to drop into the couloir's gully system, anchored on two pitons with some newish tat, and noted a full 60m rope would get a party through everything in one rappel rather than needing to downclimb the remainder — but again, this is describing getting into the route, not descending from the summit. Because the descent is the shared East Ridge walk-off, treat glacier crevasse hazard and knife-edge icing exactly as on that route, and carry a rope for the glacier crossings regardless of whether any rappelling was used higher on the mountain.
overview: The Northwest Ice Couloir splits the northwest face of Eldorado above the wild Marble Creek Cirque, offering 2-3 long pitches (often simul-climbed) up the couloir to a flat shoulder just below the summit's famous knife-edge ridge — a steeper, more technical alternative to the standard East Ridge, reached via a long and fairly complex glaciated traverse around the mountain.
bivyNames: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

pins.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of pavement on the Mountain Loop Highway, elev. ~2,361 ft, 30.5 mi east of Granite Falls), the approach starts on the gated Monte Cristo Road/Old Monte Cristo Townsite Trail — a flat, easy old railroad grade that parallels the South Fork Sauk River for about 4.1 miles to the Monte Cristo ghost town (elev. ~2,750–2,800 ft). This stretch is closed to public vehicles (maintained by volunteers) and has been damaged by past flood events: the original bridge over the South Fork Sauk near the townsite was destroyed, so expect to either ford a side channel (safe in low water, hazardous during rain/snowmelt) or cross on a fallen log — check current conditions before relying on either. From the townsite, pick up the Glacier Basin Trail, climbing steadily alongside Glacier Creek through forest; roughly the last half-mile below Glacier Basin becomes rough, rocky scrambling near a series of waterfalls (Glacier Falls). Leave the maintained trail around 4,200–4,500 ft, just above the falls, where Glacier Creek is easily and safely accessible — this is the last reliable water before the climb. From there it's cross-country travel: traverse talus and heather benches, then steep, brushy timber, toward Foggy Peak's south face/west ridge. Snowline commonly sits near 5,000 ft into early summer, so an ice axe (and possibly light crampons) is worth carrying for the upper approach in June/early July. The final few hundred feet to the summit is a steep class 3 gully with abundant loose, downsloping rock and some route-finding needed to stay at class 3 rather than straying into class 4 terrain; a helmet is strongly recommended for anyone climbing behind another party member. One-way distance from Barlow Pass to the summit is roughly 8 miles with about 4,000-4,400 ft of cumulative elevation gain, consistent with the ~25.75 km (16 mi) round-trip distance.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — down the same loose class 3 summit gully with care (loose rock and downsloping holds make down-climbing the crux, more than the ascent), then back across the talus/heather benches and through the steep brushy timber to rejoin Glacier Creek and the Glacier Basin Trail around 4,200–4,500 ft, out to Monte Cristo townsite, and back down the old road/railroad grade to Barlow Pass. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required and there are no fixed anchors or rappel stations on this route. In early season, parties often glissade lingering snow patches on the upper mountain where safe to speed the descent, then downclimb the rock below the snowline. The primary descent hazards are rockfall in the loose gully (stay tight as a group and be deliberate about not kicking rock onto anyone below), the slippery/loose scree and downsloping rock on the upper mountain, and the tedious, brush-choked steep forest lower down. Rappels: 0.
overview: Foggy Peak (6,810 ft) is a Class 3-4 scramble rising immediately northeast of the historic Monte Cristo townsite in the Monte Cristo group, within the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. It is reached via the Glacier Basin Trail (#719) out of Monte Cristo — not via Poodle Dog Pass/Silver Lake Trail (#708), which departs the townsite to the south toward Silvertip and Columbia Peaks and does not access Foggy Peak. The standard route climbs the peak's south face to its west ridge, finishing at a skyline notch just below the summit, with views of Cadet, Kyes, Sloan, and the rest of the Monte Cristo group.
bivyNames: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill

name: East Ledges
approach: Start at the Boston Basin trailhead off the Cascade River Road. A steep climbers' trail with several creek crossings (Boston Creek can run high on warm afternoons) climbs to the camps in Boston Basin; overnight stays there need a park backcountry permit. From the upper basin, head north toward Forbidden's South Face and climb the snow slopes and loose gully below and right of it to the East Ridge saddle just northwest of the Solitary Gendarme, about 8,300–8,400 ft. Allow about 4 hours from the trailhead to the saddle, or about 2 hours from the basin camps. Axe and crampons are usually needed for this snow; late in the season they can be left at the saddle.
descent: The usual descent is the ascent line reversed. From a horn near the summit, make the first of five single-rope rappels (roughly 400 ft total) down the northeast side to a series of ledges, then follow the ledges east - mostly 3rd class with short 4th-class moves at rib crossings - across roughly five rock ribs before a short gully leads back up to the East Ridge crest near the solitary gendarme. There is no easy way off Forbidden Peak - this line is unprotectable in places and has had a fatality (1975) on the ledge traverse. Cairns (a higher and lower option at most rib crossings) mark the easiest line; recent parties describe the terrain as more straightforward than its reputation suggests when the cairned line is followed carefully, but conditions and route-finding difficulty vary by party experience and weather. From the gendarme, continue down the East Ridge's standard gully system to Boston Basin.
overview: The East Ledges (also called the 'NE Ledge' in older and casual usage - a naming overlap that has caused confusion with the distinct, genuinely technical Northeast Face ice route on the same aspect) is technically the easiest route to the summit of Forbidden Peak, at Class 4. From the East Ridge saddle beside the Solitary Gendarme it drops briefly onto the north side, traverses a long band of grassy, rubbly ledges across about five rock ribs, then climbs the small northeast face directly below the summit. What it lacks in difficulty it makes up in consequence: most of the ground is exposed, sloping and cannot reliably be protected, so a slip on the ledges is likely to be fatal, and a party must be comfortable moving unroped on 3rd- and 4th-class terrain. The same line, reversed with rappels on the upper face, is the most commonly used descent off the summit for parties who climbed the West Ridge, East Ridge Direct, North Ridge or Northeast Face.

name: Northeast Face
approach: From Boston Basin Trailhead, hike ~3-4 mi via old mine road then a climbers' path (4 stream crossings) to high camp near 6,400 ft (3-4 hrs). Continue along the moraine and west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col (~7,720 ft) via ~10 ft of 5.7 rock and a Class 3 gully. Rappel into the bergschrund on the far side and climb a short ice wall to gain the Boston Glacier, then traverse west across the Boston Glacier to the base of the Northeast Face below a prominent ice patch.
descent: Do not reverse the Northeast Face. Most parties descend by the West Ridge, as below; the East Ledges off the northeast side are the faster but looser, harder-to-follow alternative. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the West Ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the notch between Forbidden and Torment. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. From the base, cross back to Boston Basin camp and hike out the climbers' trail. This is a long day; budget extra time given the remote, less-travelled ascent line.
overview: A steep face of rock and ice on the northeast side of Forbidden Peak: rock below and above a single steep ice patch (about 50°) in the middle of the face. Best in firm early-season conditions, it is a rarely climbed line in a shaded, remote North Cascades cirque.
bivyNames: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins

name: Wilkes-Booth (Northwest Face)
approach: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (FS Road 39, Trail #677) near Glacier, WA, and follow the Heliotrope Ridge Trail roughly 2 miles through old-growth forest and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site (~4,700 ft). From Heliotrope Ridge, cross the lower Thunder Glacier to the base of Lincoln's northwest face and the prominent hanging glacier, where the route starts at the same point as the routes on Assassin Spire. Rope up for the glacier; the face is big and complex and cannot be seen whole from the approach.
descent: Descend the southwest face route: roughly 2,000 ft of steep snow and ice up to 65°, downclimbed in good conditions and otherwise rappelled. Below the face, traverse back along the north side of the peak toward Heliotrope Ridge, roped for the glacier, and walk out the Heliotrope Ridge Trail.
overview: Wilkes-Booth climbs about 2,000 ft of glacial, alpine and water ice on Lincoln Peak's northwest face, with steep snowfields between the ice and a rime-covered ridge to finish. Its first pitch, a 60 m WI4 lead with overhanging, poorly protected ice in its upper half, is the crux and is shared with the lines on Assassin Spire. The route depends on unusually good ice build-up; the first ascent was a single 18.5-hour push from the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead in a one-day March weather window, descending the southwest face.

pins.name: NW Face start / hanging glacier icefall

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Four approaches reach Monument Peak, all long and remote — this is deep in the Pasayten Wilderness near the Canadian border, and most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a high camp. The most common is via the Monument Creek Trailhead on Lost River Road/FR 5400 (about 22 miles northwest of Winthrop via Mazama), starting at roughly 2,400 ft. From the trailhead, follow Monument Creek Trail No. 484 up the Lost River valley; the first ~4 miles are well-maintained through old-growth forest and along rock slopes to the Eureka Creek confluence (Eureka Falls Camp) — this is your last easy, reliable water before a long dry stretch. Beyond Eureka Creek the trail has been essentially unmaintained for 25+ years, brushy and choked with deadfall, and route-finding becomes real work. Ford Eureka Creek (can run thigh-to-waist deep during snowmelt — a genuine early-summer hazard) then pick up the abandoned tread climbing onto Pistol Ridge, following it up to 7,100-ft Pistol Pass around mile 11. From the pass, descend about a mile on the trail, finishing on a short spur, to Lake of the Woods in the Monument–Lake Mountain basin, a common high camp — about 12 miles and 5,300 ft of gain from the trailhead. From camp, traverse cross-country northwest to the ~7,400-ft saddle below Lake Mountain, then descend into Lower Monument Basin (~6,100 ft); the lake-outlet creek here is your last dependable water for the summit push and can shrink to a trickle late in the season. From the basin, climb a left-angling ramp system to gain Monument Peak's south/southeast ridge at about 6,900 ft, then follow a long talus traverse toward the summit. The final section involves roughly a half-pitch of Class 3 (locally Class 3-4) scrambling where the ridge merges with the southeast slopes, sometimes complicated by a steep snowfield just below the true summit that can still require an ice axe (or a class 3/4 rock detour around its left side) into midsummer. Three alternative approaches exist: dropping in from 6,960-ft Slate Pass on the Harts Pass Road down to the Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 and Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A (reportedly the easiest, though not shortest, reaching the same basin from the north); via the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead just past Harts Pass on Trail No. 498, crossing the Middle Fork Pasayten River and picking up Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 then Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A; or a longer approach from the Lost Creek/Monument Creek trailhead side. Whichever line is used, expect long, remote travel with significant off-trail brush and route-finding on the final miles — carry a map/GPS and budget extra time.
descent: This is a walk-off — there is no rappelling on the standard scramble route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 3 (occasionally 3-4) rock/talus off the summit block to regain the south/southeast ridge at roughly 6,900 ft, then descend the left-angling ramp system back into Lower Monument Basin, topping off water at the lake-outlet creek if needed, before climbing back up to the Lake Mountain saddle (~7,400 ft) and dropping to high camp at Lake of the Woods. Where a summit snowfield was crossed on the ascent, most parties recross it on foot (or skirt around its left side on rock) rather than glissade, since it can remain firm or icy well into summer. The main descent hazards are loose talus, exposed Class 3 scrambling near the summit, and route-finding fatigue — several parties describe finishing the final talus slopes back to camp by headlamp. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel gear are used on this route. From camp, retrace whichever approach trail was used — Pistol Pass and the Eureka Creek ford back to the Monument Creek Trailhead, or the Ferguson Lake/Robinson Creek trail back to Slate Pass or the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead — to reach the road.
overview: Monument Peak is the most rugged and inaccessible peak in the Lago group, deep in the eastern Pasayten Wilderness near the Eureka Creek country. Double-nubbed and built of granite, it sits almost as an island: Eureka Creek wraps its north, west, and south sides while Monument Creek drains the east side. The mountain has a precipitous north/northeast side, a cliffy east face, a rugged west face, and a comparatively gentler (though still remote) south slope that forms the standard scramble line. A disheveled connecting ridge links it to 8,397-ft Blackcap Mountain a half-mile north; 8,745-ft Mount Lago, its line parent, lies about 2.4 miles further north. First ascended in 1978 by Fred Beckey and John Roper.
bivyNames: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp

name: East Route / Standard
approach: Start at the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft), reached via the rough spur road off SR-20 near milepost 117. Follow the Thornton Lakes Trail/old roadbed on a nearly flat first mile to a crossing of Thornton Creek — the last reliable, easy water source before the route goes fully off-trail. From the creek, leave the maintained tread and begin bushwhacking up-slope: expect a series of small cliff bands that force a leftward (northerly) traverse through thickets of slide alder, then a ferny talus slope above a 3,800-ft hanging meadow, followed by a steep, brushy push of about 1,000 ft through cedar limbs and heavy brush to a rocky shoulder at roughly 5,300 ft on Thornton Ridge. Budget most of a day for this stretch alone (parties have taken 7+ hours from trailhead to the shoulder) — it is the crux of the approach in terms of effort and route-finding, not the climbing itself. From the Thornton Ridge shoulder, traverse north over rock and heather, working around minor terrain obstacles, to flat benches near 6,050-ft Thornton Pass — the standard camp for this route (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip rather than a car-to-car push). From camp, descend back to about 5,300 ft and cross roughly 1.5 hours of shoulder-high brush to a cascading stream with open bedrock slabs (a second water source); down-climb the slabs about 200 ft, then drop through forest and steep duff for another 500 ft to about 4,600 ft. Traverse into the open basin below Triumph Pass and climb to the 5,500-ft pass. From Triumph Pass, descend a north-facing snowfield to about 4,900 ft, skirt Lake Regret (often partly frozen) on its west-side moraine, then re-climb to roughly 5,300 ft and traverse several miles of heather benches, slabs, and shallow ravines to 5,100-ft Upper Despair Lake. From the lake, climb a heathery ridge to the east, then talus and snow, to reach the cliff band directly below Despair's southeast face/east ridge, where the technical climbing begins. Total approach mileage/gain to this point is substantial — trip reports covering the full round trip (trailhead to summit and back) log roughly 24 miles and 12,000+ ft of cumulative gain and loss, consistent with this route's recorded ~38.6 km distance. Key hazards: creek crossing at Thornton Creek (usually a rock-hop, can be pushier in early season snowmelt); loose, vegetated rock in the cliff bands above Thornton Creek; extended off-trail travel with real route-finding consequences (parties have gotten cliffed out and had to backtrack); and lingering snow patches/steep snow chutes near Despair Lakes into early summer.
descent: The 'standard'/East Route descent reverses the east ridge on which most modern parties actually climb (rather than the steeper southeast-face dihedral line some early parties used). This is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route: parties who instead climbed the SE-face dihedral variant found they had to rappel that single pitch to get back onto the ridge, then realized the East Ridge itself offers an easy, continuous Class 3 downclimb that avoids rope work entirely — this is why it's now treated as the standard descent. From the summit, downclimb the east ridge (Class 3, exposed but not technical) back to the cliff band above Upper Despair Lake; if that band is wet or a party prefers not to downclimb it, a single short rappel (roughly a half rope-length, natural gear/sling anchor off a horn or block — no fixed/bolted anchors are reported on this remote route) is a reasonable fallback, but it is not required under normal dry conditions. From the cliff band, reverse the approach: back down to Upper Despair Lake, across the multi-mile heather/slab/ravine traverse to the Lake Regret moraine, up and over the north-facing snowfield to Triumph Pass, down into the basin, back up the steep duff/slab down-climb section to about 5,300 ft, over Thornton Ridge, and down through the brush and cliff bands to Thornton Creek and the trailhead. Parties doing this in a single push from camp report full days (12+ hours) with the final stretch through talus and brush often finishing in the dark — bring headlamps and expect the descent to take as long as or longer than the ascent given the sustained off-trail terrain. No fixed rappel stations exist on this route; any rope use is opportunistic (natural anchors) rather than an established rappel line.
overview: Mount Despair is a remote, twin-summited granite peak in the North Unit of North Cascades National Park, its glaciated cirques draining north into Bacon Creek and south into Goodell Creek. Named by USFS surveyor Lage Wernstedt in the 1920s (the name first appeared on Forest Service maps in 1931), it saw its first ascent in 1939 by a 16-year-old Fred Beckey and two companions. The peak sits in the same remote, trail-less cluster as Mount Triumph, Mount Terror, and Bacon Peak, and is known among North Cascades climbers less for technical difficulty on the summit block than for its long, brushy, multi-day approach via Thornton Lakes and Triumph Pass.

name: Standard Route
approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel.
descent: This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, descend the Southwest Ridge, circle back around the north side of the peak and reclimb the Carrie Glacier roped up with crampons to Mount Carrie's summit, then descend Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill back across Carrie's south face (or take the north-side alternative), then recross the Catwalk to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.
overview: Mount Fairchild (6,899 ft) is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range, a glaciated subrange deep in the interior of Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It carries the small, retreating Fairchild Glacier on its northeast flank and sits about 0.84 mi northeast of higher neighbor Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). No trail comes anywhere close to the summit — nearly all ascents are made as a side-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone climb, and the peak sees only a handful of ascents most years. First climbed in 1963 by Denny Pruitt, Dan Baker, Jack Christiansen, and Roy Etten.

name: Standard Scramble (South/East Slopes)
approach: Start from the Bagley Lakes Trailhead (~4,200 ft) at the south end of the upper Mt. Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 684.1) south along the eastern shore of Bagley Lake — this is the only reliable water source on the route, and it should still be filtered/treated. At about 0.75 mile, the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 682), which bends west and begins switchbacking up toward Herman Saddle (~5,300 ft), roughly 1.5-2 miles and about 1,100 ft above the lakes. Snow frequently lingers on this slope into July or even August, and the Forest Service explicitly flags it as avalanche terrain in winter/spring conditions, so check current conditions before an early-season trip; poles and some route-finding are recommended even on the maintained tread. At the last switchback below Herman Saddle — the low point on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome (west) and Mount Herman (east) — leave the maintained trail and go cross-country, climbing open heather slopes and a short band of scrub trees for a couple hundred vertical feet to gain the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge. This off-trail stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach; the correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility. Once on the ridge, follow its crest generally eastward, staying mostly on the south/southwest side over heather benches and loose scree/talus, to the base of a short final east ridge that leads to the true summit at 6,285 ft.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent descent route. Downclimb the short summit east ridge back to the south/southwest ridge, then follow that ridge and its heather-and-scree slopes back down to the low saddle point between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman. Drop off the ridge on the same cross-country line through the scrub-tree band and heather slopes to rejoin the maintained Chain Lakes Trail (682) at the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then follow Chain Lakes Trail and Bagley Lakes Trail (684.1) back past Bagley Lakes to the trailhead. This is a walk-off scramble with no rappelling required under normal summer/dry conditions — 0 rappels. The main descent hazards are loose, down-sloping scree and talus on the ridge and connecting slopes (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below), and lingering snow in the gully/ridge-traverse sections in early season, where an ice axe and/or microspikes are a reasonable precaution; a rope is not standard gear for this route.
overview: An off-trail scramble above Heather Meadows on the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) — despite easy road access it is climbed far less often than neighbors like Table Mountain or Church Mountain, and is best known locally among backcountry skiers who ski/ride its couloirs. From the Bagley Lakes/Chain Lakes Trail near Herman Saddle, parties leave the maintained trail and pick a line up heather benches and scree to the south ridge, finishing on a short, loose, exposed east ridge to a summit with a 1939 USGS survey marker and views of Mount Baker, Mount Shuksan, the Pickets, and the border peaks (Larrabee, American Border Peak, Tomyhoi).

pins.name: Chain Lakes Trail — switchbacks toward Herman Saddle
Unnamed lake / gully to summit ridge

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, start on Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 through second-growth and then old-growth forest along the Dungeness River. At about 1 mile, bear right at the signed junction onto the Royal Basin Trail (the left fork continues up-valley toward Boulder Shelter/Constance Pass). The Royal Basin trail then climbs gradually for several miles alongside Royal Creek — the main water source for the approach — crossing it on log/plank bridges more than once; these crossings can run fast and cold during early-season snowmelt (June). Around mile 6 the grade steepens sharply for the push to Royal Lake (7.2 mi, roughly 2,500 ft gained from the trailhead), with the final mile gaining about 500 ft on looser, sometimes-eroded tread. From Royal Lake continue south up-valley on the scramblers'/climbers' path roughly another 0.8 mile and 600 ft to Upper Royal Basin (about 8 mi in, ~5,700 ft), a broad heather-and-tarn basin below Mount Deception's northeast face that most parties use as base camp (NPS wilderness permit and bear canister required; no fires; advance reservations cover June 15–Oct 15). From Upper Royal Basin the maintained trail ends; head cross-country west up heather benches and talus to the rim of the glacial moraine ringing Surprise Basin, the small hanging cirque between Mount Martin, Mount Johnson, and Mount Clark. Drop into Surprise Basin and cross its snowfields (crampons/axe often useful into July) toward the roughly 6,900 ft notch/col between Johnson (climber's left) and Clark (climber's right) — this is the standard gateway to Johnson's upper mountain. This off-trail stretch above Upper Royal Basin is loose talus and scree with genuine rockfall and route-finding hazard; helmets on from the moraine rim upward. Given the total distance (~19 miles / 30.9 km round trip) and elevation gain, most parties backpack in and camp at Upper Royal Basin, climbing Johnson as a long day from camp rather than attempting it car-to-car.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit back to the ~6,900 ft Johnson–Clark notch, then retrace the talus-and-moraine descent down into Surprise Basin and back over its rim to Upper Royal Basin, from which the Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail leads back out to the trailhead. The class 4 terrain near the summit is the crux of the descent as well as the ascent — the rock is loose enough in spots that most reported difficulty on this peak comes from downclimbing it, so face in and test holds on anything above class 3. The summit chimney is downclimbed rather than rappelled; there are no fixed/bolted rappel stations reported on Johnson, so a party that wants a rope on the steepest step, particularly if the rock is wet, must rig it from a natural anchor (horn, chockstone, or slung block) of its own.
overview: Mount Johnson (7,680 ft) is the fourth-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains and the highest point in The Needles, a rugged subrange radiating north from Mount Deception above Royal Basin, in the remote eastern Olympics within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It sits just 1.34 miles north of Mount Deception, its parent peak and nearest higher neighbor. Compared to well-traveled Deception, Johnson sees relatively few ascents: accounts range from an exposed class 3-4 scramble to unavoidably loose class 4 terrain, and the long interior approach through Royal Basin means most parties treat it as a multi-day trip, frequently paired with neighboring Mount Clark via the Clark-Johnson col.

name: North Face
approach: Long approach into the Entiat Mountains, via one of two options: from the Phelps Creek Trailhead, hike ~3.5 miles to the Leroy Creek crossing, then continue cross-country up to Leroy Basin and over the Seven Fingered Jack-Maude col; or drive Entiat River Road (becomes FR 51/5100) ~38 miles from Entiat to Cottonwood Campground, then hike the Entiat River Trail ~14.5 miles to the cirque below Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, and Fernow (this trail passes through terrain burned in the 2015 Wolverine Fire).
descent: The North Face is not descended — after topping out on the summit ridge (9,082 ft), descend via the standard South Slopes / south ridge walk-off: down the south ridge and upper talus to about 7,700 ft, then southwest down broad open slopes to the 6,840 ft saddle. From there most parties drop back into Leroy Creek Basin to retrieve camp and reverse the Leroy Creek climber's path and Phelps Creek Trail to the trailhead; some parties instead exit via the Ice Lakes basin and the Carne Mountain High Route depending on snow conditions and where camp/vehicles are staged, which several parties describe as an efficient alternative when the Maude/Seven Fingered Jack col has gone soft and mushy in the afternoon. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly reported on the standard descent line (the single technical rappel reported is on the approach traverse under the face, not the summit descent, and is conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route). Descent-specific hazards: loose 3rd-class rock and scree on the south ridge/upper slopes, a large cornice that forms on the summit ridge above the North Face's climber's-right side (stay well back from the edge near the top), lingering steep snow and possible rockfall in the col/gully area, and — if exiting toward Ice Lakes — extra route-finding and a longer, more remote tail to the car. Parties should budget real time for this descent; one party logged roughly 13 hours car-to-car including the North Face climb and this walk-off.
overview: The North Face is Mount Maude's classic moderate snow/ice climb: from the small Entiat Glacier at the peak's northeast base, a sustained 40-55 degree snow (occasionally alpine ice) face rises roughly 4,000 vertical feet to finish roughly 100 vertical feet below the summit. It has long been one of the more popular moderate alpine snow climbs in the Entiat Mountains, though continuous snow/ice coverage has become less reliable as the glacier has retreated in recent decades.

name: South Slopes
approach: Start at the Stafford Creek Trailhead (Trail #1359), Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the end of Stafford Creek Road (FR 9703), which leaves North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) past 29 Pines Campground — a small, often-overflowing lot for roughly 20 cars (Northwest Forest Pass required). From the trailhead, Stafford Creek Trail #1359 climbs at a gentle-to-moderate grade through dry ponderosa/lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek for the first mile (a short rerouted, steeper switchback section around 0.5 mile bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread). The trail continues gaining gradually along the creek — figure roughly 3,000 ft of gain spread over the approach — reaching a signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) at about 3.5–3.8 miles; this crossing of Stafford Creek is the last reliable, easy water source before the high country and is worth topping off here. Bear right (east/north) at the junction to stay on the Navaho Pass approach. Around 4.5 miles the trail opens into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with established campsites and a feeder stream — the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days, and another water source. Beyond camp the trail crosses the barren, eroded 'Moon Landing' stretch (sparse vegetation, serpentine/greenstone talus) before a final push to Navaho Pass (~6,000 ft) around mile 5.5. A commonly used shortcut leaves the main trail where two creek forks merge around the 3-mile mark, climbing steep, loose slopes directly up the northeast-facing drainage to the col below Navaho's southeast ridge — it saves close to 2 miles of trail hiking but is steeper, unmaintained, and involves loose scree/dirt, so most parties use it only for one direction of the trip. Total car-to-summit is on the order of 11–13 miles round trip with about 4,000–4,200 ft of gain depending on which junction/shortcut combination is used. Note: several miles of this trail burned in the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire. Its closure order has been lifted and the trail is open, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026, but expect burned forest and dead trees along the corridor. A second off-trail variant leaves the trail right after the Stafford Creek crossing and climbs directly into the open bowl between Earl Peak and Navaho Peak to about 5,000 ft, scrambles north to the ridgeline near 6,000 ft, then follows the west/southwest ridge to the summit — a different line than the northeast-drainage shortcut.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: drop off the summit back down the broad south/southeast ridge to Navaho Pass (easy Class 2 scrambling, no rope or rappelling needed), then rejoin Stafford Creek Trail #1359 and retrace it past the Moon Landing section, the meadow camp/water source, the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) junction at ~3.5–3.8 miles, and back down along Stafford Creek to the trailhead. Parties who used the creek-fork shortcut on the way up sometimes descend the standard pass-and-trail route instead (or vice versa) to make a rough loop, but both options are plain hiking/scrambling terrain — there is no rappelling on this route. Watch for loose scree and dirt on the steeper shortcut drainage if descending that way, and expect possible lingering snow near the pass and on the upper ridge into early-mid summer, which can make the descent line slicker than the ascent.
overview: Navaho Peak is the fourth-highest summit in the Teanaway high country and sits on the boundary of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, on the Kittitas/Chelan county line about 2 miles northeast of Earl Peak and 1.3 miles west of Three Brothers. The South Slopes/Southwest Ridge line is the standard non-technical route: a long approach up Stafford Creek to an open bowl and ridge system, then a broad talus-and-heather scramble to a small summit (room for only 4-5 people) with wide views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, Sherpa Peak, Earl Peak, and Mount Rainier.
bivyNames: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass

name: North Face (Beckey-Schmidtke Route)
approach: From Bellingham, exit Interstate 5 at Sunset Drive/Mount Baker exit. Drive Mount Baker Highway (Washington 542) east through the town of Glacier (last resupply for groceries) and continue 13 miles to the Nooksack River bridge. Immediately before the bridge, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (USFS #32). Stay left at 0.5 miles, then bear right onto Nooksack Cirque Road (#34) at about 1.4 miles from highway. Continue to the washout at 2.3 miles from the highway and park at Ruth Creek (elevation 2,156 feet). Hike the abandoned road beyond the washout for two miles to the original Nooksack Cirque trailhead at 2,550 feet. River ford the Nooksack (use the log crossing at the original location noted at N48.87097 W121.61267; new logs are often swept away). Proceed up the forested mountainside east of the creek, starting up the west bank of Price Creek until finding a good log crossing. Continue to the moraine above Price Lake (3,911 feet), then hike the ridgeline between Price and East Nooksack Glaciers upward from the moraine to a rock slab bivouac spot at approximately 5,900 feet. From the bivouac, gain the glacier, traverse climber's right along the glacier to an exposed snow saddle below Nooksack Tower, then drop down and work onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier.
descent: Beckey and Schmidtke's 1946 descent reversed the route: an uneventful series of rappels from pitons placed in the rock wall flanking the couloir, back down to the glacier and camp. Modern parties do the same — this route is a there-and-back climb, reversed rather than continuing over the summit. From the top, downclimb/rappel the north arête and rock trough back to the head of the couloir, then make a long series of rappels (parties describe roughly ten 60m rappels) down the couloir to the snow/glacier below, building anchors as needed (slings on rock horns, occasional picket or v-thread — don't count on finding fixed gear in place or trustworthy). Where conditions allow, the lower couloir is often downclimbed instead of rappelled. From the base of the couloir, reverse the approach across the glacier/basin to the bivy, then down through Price Lake, the forested slope, and the Nooksack River flats to the Ruth Creek trailhead. Because the descent is technical, parties are frequently still on the couloir or lower approach after dark — one party describes getting back to camp roughly 21 hours after leaving it. Unlike the Price Glacier route, no car shuttle is needed — this returns to the same Ruth Creek trailhead.
overview: A dramatic and serious rock spire on the northeast side of Mount Shuksan's main massif, ringed by the Price, East Nooksack, and West Nooksack Glaciers, Nooksack Tower is one of the more committing summits in the North Cascades, with a reputation for loose rock and a demanding approach. The North Face (Beckey-Schmidtke) route is the classic line, first climbed in 1946 by Fred Beckey and Cliff Schmidtke.
bivyNames: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower

pins.name: Off-trail ford of the Nooksack River

name: NW Ridge
approach: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) and the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) from the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road) — 4 miles and 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles and staying left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction — to reach Colchuck Lake (2.5-3 hours). Unlike the west-side routes, the NW Ridge is approached from the east side of the lake: work around the eastern shoreline/talus to the base of the obvious gully that splits toward the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, the granite spire between the lake and Colchuck Balanced Rock. Ascend this gully (loose in spots, rope-up terrain for the upper section) to the notch, then move onto class-3 ground on the NW Ridge proper before the climbing begins. One documented ascent clocked roughly 4,760 ft of total gain and a 12-hour car-to-car day, consistent with the route's ~18.5 km round-trip distance.
descent: From the ridge's high point (below the exposed summit boulder problem, which most parties do not attempt due to thin protection), descend via a single ~25m rappel down the east face off a fixed anchor — a natural sling/horn setup rather than bolts, so inspect it before committing. After the rappel, scramble down talus and broken rock slopes, contouring around to a saddle on the south side, back past Jabberwocky Tower, and down to Colchuck Lake to rejoin the standard hike-out. Loose rock and route-finding through the talus are the main descent hazards; this is not a walk in fading light without a headlamp given the boulder-hopping involved.
overview: A moderate scramble/low-5th-class ridge route on the northwest side of the formation, approached from the east side of Colchuck Lake. Class 3 terrain leads to a notch above Jabberwocky Tower, followed by a few pitches of low 5th class up to 5.6 along the exposed ridge crest to the summit area.
bivyNames: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road

name: Southwest Rib
approach: From Blue Lake Trailhead (1 mile west of Washington Pass on Highway 20), hike Blue Lake Trail 1.25-1.5 miles to a clearing. At a small stream (possibly marked with cairns), leave the trail and ascend climber tracks through slabs parallel to the stream to reach the basin. Route base is identifiable by the distinctive Y-shaped larch tree. Total approach time: 1-1.5 hours; elevation gain to route base: 900-1,200 ft.
descent: Descend via the South Arete (the standard descent for the peak): downclimbing 3rd/4th class terrain to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors back toward the Blue Lake basin. Expect delays at rappel stations on busy weekends since South Arete parties are often descending the same line.
overview: The Southwest Rib is one of the most popular moderate multipitch alpine rock climbs at Washington Pass, climbing excellent granite on the west face of South Early Winter Spire with a famous dual-offwidth Bear Hug pitch and an airy slabby arete.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FS Road 4065), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (#707) into the Morning Star NRCA. About 0.5 mile in, the trail makes a tricky crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish River — no bridge, sometimes aided by a small-diameter log and a hand rope; this ford can be genuinely difficult and dangerous after heavy rain or early-season snowmelt. Beyond the crossing the trail climbs gradually through forest for roughly a mile to Wirtz Basin, where the terrain opens up and turns rockier. From the basin the trail steepens sharply into a narrow, loose rock chute switchbacking up to Headlee Pass (4,720 ft, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead) — this chute is notorious for rockfall dislodged by parties above and is also an avalanche path in shoulder-season/spring snow conditions, so groups should spread out and move through it deliberately. From Headlee Pass the trail contours around Sperry's south/east flank and drops slightly into the upper Vesper Creek basin to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, roughly 3 miles in). Leave the maintained trail at the lake's outlet, follow its east shore, then climb open, welcoming slopes to the saddle/notch between Vesper and Sperry Peaks (Sperry Saddle). From the saddle it's off-trail scrambling up Sperry's west ridge/west slope — loose, often wet dirt and heather with class 3 rock steps, including some brushy, tree-assisted moves in the final push to the summit block — to the 6,120 ft summit. Total distance to the top is around 4 miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain; water is available at the South Fork crossing and at Vesper Lake but not much beyond it, so top off before leaving the lake.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose, brushy west ridge/west slope scramble back to Sperry Saddle, then drop to the Vesper Lake outlet and rejoin the maintained Sunrise Mine Trail. Route-finding on the upper scramble is the main hazard on the way down — the easiest line up is not obvious from above, and it's easy to end up descending a different, steeper gully than the one you climbed, so note landmarks (the climber's-right ramp and the cairned dirt path into the trees) on the way up and look for them again on the way down. From the lake, retrace the trail back through Headlee Pass and down its rockfall-prone switchback chute (loose underfoot, stay alert for rock knocked loose by other parties), through Wirtz Basin, back across the South Fork Stillaguamish ford, and out to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no rappelling involved anywhere on the standard line.
overview: Sperry Peak (6,120+ ft, USGS contour interval; some LIDAR-based lists cite ~6,140 ft) sits directly across the Sunrise Mine basin from Vesper Peak, rising over 3,900 ft above the South Fork Stillaguamish in about a mile. It's a straightforward-looking but sneaky Class 2-3 scramble on talus, heather benches and low-angle slab, with a loose, sustained, and routefinding-heavy final push to a small summit. Named for A. D. "Dick" Sperry, an 1890s Silverton mining prospector; first ascended in 1927 by Norval Grigg and Art Winder.

name: Southeast Route / Standard
approach: Primary approach (White River side): From Hwy 2 at Coles Corner, follow Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (Forest Road 6400) to its end at the White River/Indian Creek Trailhead (~2,300 ft). Hike the White River Trail #1507 about 6 miles to the Thunder Creek crossing. A half mile past Thunder Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up an old, unmaintained sheep trail that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage through avalanche debris and brush to a lower basin (~4,175 ft), then steeply up to the upper Thunder Basin (~5,180 ft, about 9 miles and 2,900 ft above the trailhead) — the standard high camp with a direct view of Tenpeak. Alternate approach (North Fork Sauk / west side): drive the Mountain Loop Highway to Forest Road 49 and the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,100 ft), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country via Boulder Pass and the Napeequa Valley to Tenpeak's north/northeast side — a much longer, more committing option (reported as ~31 miles and 13,500 ft of gain over 3 days for a full traverse) with 20+ stream crossings and dense brush. From the Thunder Basin camp, the route continues across talus and snow to a col east of the summit block (ice axe/crampons typically needed for the sometimes-firm snow), then climbs a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system, followed by a broken chimney/face pitch (Class 4 to easy Class 5 depending on conditions) to the summit; rock in the gully and chimney is loose, so helmet up and manage rope/party spacing to avoid dropping rock on others below.
descent: Rappel or downclimb the chimney and the gully to the col, then reverse the snow and talus to Thunder Basin.
overview: Tenpeak Mountain is a rugged, partly glaciated 8,312' summit in the Dakobed Range, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness southeast of Glacier Peak itself. Cretaceous-age granitic rock, small hanging glaciers on its flanks, and a 4,200-ft north face dropping to the Suiattle Valley give it real alpine character despite its modest elevation. First ascended September 21, 1940 by Lloyd Anderson and Tom Campbell via essentially this same Southeast Slope line. It is a low-traffic objective — most parties reach it via a long, largely cross-country approach from the White River Trailhead near Lake Wenatchee (Chelan County side) or, less commonly, from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead off the Mountain Loop Highway (Snohomish County side).

name: South Slopes
approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road and follow the maintained trail over Cascade Pass and down the Stehekin side to Pelton Basin. From the lowest tent sites at Pelton Basin, leave the trail on a faint boot path dropping toward Pelton Creek; below that the fisherman's path to Trapper Lake appears and vanishes, so expect route-finding through brush and alder before a flat, marshy walk along the inlet stream to the lake. Most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip with a camp at Trapper Lake. The lake can also be reached by a steep off-trail climb from the upper Stehekin valley, but that line is harder to locate and first requires reaching Stehekin by boat or floatplane.
descent: Descend by reversing the south-slopes/basin ascent line back to Trapper Lake; no rappels are needed on the standard route. Loose talus and heather benches call for careful footing, especially late in the day when upper slopes have softened or afternoon thunderstorms are building.
overview: Trapper Mountain (7,530 ft) rises on the crest of the North Cascades southeast of Cascade Pass, on the shared boundary of North Cascades National Park and the Glacier Peak Wilderness, about 0.7 mile east of Hurry-up Peak (7,821 ft) near the head of the Ptarmigan Traverse country. Runoff from the peak's basin and small glacial remnant feeds Trapper Lake and tributaries of the Stehekin River. It is a genuinely remote, seldom-visited scramble — access is a trail hike over Cascade Pass followed by a long off-trail bushwhack down to Trapper Lake — so parties can expect real solitude even in peak season. First climbed in 1949 by George Bell, Andrew Griscom, Harry King, and W. V. Graham Matthews.

name: Windy Peak Trail (Standard Walk-up)
approach: From Tonasket, cross the Okanogan River and drive west on Loomis-Oroville Road to Loomis. Just north of town, turn onto Toats Coulee Road (County Rd #9425, becoming #4066 then FR-39) and follow it roughly 20 miles to the junction with FR-3900-300 at Long Swamp Campground — the standard trailhead for Windy Peak Trail #342. The Windy Creek/Cathedral Driveway trailhead is about 3 miles farther west on the same road system; the separate Iron Gate trailhead is reached via a rougher spur and has the roughest driving of the three approaches (last ~6 miles).
descent: Reverse the ascent trail (out-and-back). A loop via the Iron Gate/Horseshoe Basin trail system is possible instead of retracing the Long Swamp trail, but requires a car shuttle or significant extra road walking.
overview: Windy Peak (8,335') is the easternmost of Washington's 100 highest peaks (the "Bulgers"), standing over the remote northeastern Pasayten Wilderness about 5 miles south of the Canadian border. Unlike most Bulgers, its standard route is a non-technical trail walk-up rather than a climb — it's cataloged here for peakbagging-list completeness, and the real challenge is logistical: a long, remote approach on gravel forest roads far from any town. A gabled-roof L-4 cab fire lookout was built on the summit in 1932 by E.W. Allen and Raymond Johnson, saw brief use in the WWII Aircraft Warning Service (Jul-Sep 1942), and was removed in 1963; remnants of its old telephone line are still visible on the northwest slope.
